_about: The blood hub (plan 7.6f, third round). One word family, the Hebrew דָּם (292 verses in the lexicon's count) and the Greek αἷμα (90), with αἱματεκχυσία 'shedding of blood' (Heb 9:22, its only verse). There is no verb of the family, and the rows are not made by who does what to whom: they are made by what the verse is about, in the text's own words. The card's own four verses (Gen 9:4-6, Job 16:18) are life and bloodshed; the rest of the Bible says more: the blood of the rites, the blood of the covenant, the cup, and the blood a person is guilty of. The rows are mostly by hand through 'add' or 'pick': 'add' keeps a verse only where the builder sees the blood word in it (so a mistyped reference falls out instead of showing a verse without the word); 'pick' is used where the builder cannot see the word (Heb 9:14 and Luke 11:51, whose clause the word-by-word text files under the verse before) and every picked verse was read in the Berean. A few rows are by rule (the rites, the atonement words, the covenant words). A verse sits in every row it fits (match: all). The rows run from life (the blood speaks; the life is in it; flesh and blood; a flow of blood), through bloodshed (shed, guilt, avenged, war), the sign, the rites, to what the blood does (in the alphabetical order of the labels, so no order suggests a ranking), the covenant and the cup, and the blood of Christ. The senses the English 'blood' keeps together are kept apart by row: blood as life; blood as bloodshed and blood-guilt (the same Hebrew word, often in the plural, which the Berean prints 'bloodshed' and 'bloodguilt'); blood in the rites; the blood of Christ; and blood as a sign and a figure (water to blood, the moon to blood, flesh and blood, the sword drinking blood). The contested points (what the blood does; the blood of the covenant; the Lord's cup; the eating of blood) are set out as rows of the text's own words, each with a note that the page takes no side. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/blood.json.

titles.noun: What the text says of blood

_words_why: דָּם and αἷμα, together because the Greek Old Testament renders the one by the other and the New Testament quotes it so (Heb 9:20 quotes Exod 24:8), but the hub never says they are one word: every example names the word it stands on. αἱματεκχυσία (Heb 9:22) is the compound 'blood-shedding' the card lists in its family; its one verse also has αἷμα. Left out as a different word: αἱμορροέω 'to bleed' (g131, Matt 9:20, the woman with the flow of blood), which has no word for blood in its verse; it is named under 'Other words' and the same story is in 'A flow of blood' through Mark 5:25 and Luke 8:43-44, where αἷμα stands. The Hebrew דָּם is also the 'blood' of bloodshed in the plural (דָּמִים): one lemma, many senses, kept apart by the rows and not by the word. נֶפֶשׁ 'life, soul' sits beside blood in Gen 9:4 and Lev 17:11 and is a different word.
_sense_why: Empty, as holiness and covenant: every use of דָּם and αἷμα is the one word, whether the Berean prints blood, bloodshed, bloodguilt or lifeblood, and the rows divide the uses by what the verse is about. Measured: 292 of 292 Hebrew verses and 90 of 90 Greek verses kept, none dropped. A gloss rule would have dropped the bloodshed verses ('bloodguilt', 'bloodshed') that the Hebrew puts in the same word as the altar's blood. Two verses where the Berean has no 'blood' are kept and told in 'Every other use': Lev 19:16 ('the life of your neighbor') and Ezek 19:10 ('vineyard').

others._why: Words the English also renders blood or bloodshed that are not דָּם or αἷμα, named apart with their verses and never handed over as the same word. Found by the builder: מִשְׂפָּח (Isa 5:7, 'bloodshed', a play on 'justice' in the same verse), αἱμορροέω (Matt 9:20, 'bleeding'), עֶצֶם 'bone' (2 Sam 5:1) and מֵעִים 'inward parts' (2 Sam 16:11), both printed 'flesh and blood'. Added by hand on the panel's word (2026-10-25): notes on the last two, and נֵצַח (Isa 63:3), the winepress verse.
others.title: Other words translated “blood”, “bloodshed”, “bleeding”

h6106.note: עֶצֶם “bone” is the Hebrew of kinship in 2 Sam 5:1, where the tribes say to David “your bone and your flesh”; the Berean prints “your own flesh and blood”, and the page does not make it the word דָּם.

h4578.note: מֵעִים “inward parts” is the Hebrew in 2 Sam 16:11, where David says his son came out of his inward parts; the Berean prints “my own flesh and blood”, and the page does not make it the word דָּם.

h5332.note: נֵצַח (“juice”) is a different Hebrew word from דָּם; the Berean prints it “blood” in the winepress of Isa 63:3, “their blood spattered My garments”. Readers set it beside Rev 14:20 and 19:13 (the winepress; a robe dipped in blood), and the page does not make it the word דָּם.

h4939.note: מִשְׂפָּח (found only here) is the Berean's “bloodshed” in “He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed”; the Hebrew sets it beside מִשְׁפָּט “justice”, and the page does not make it the word דָּם.

g131.note: αἱμορροέω means “to have a flow of blood”; the Berean prints “bleeding”. It is the verb of the story Mark 5:25 and Luke 8:43-44 tell with the noun αἷμα, which is in this hub's “A flow of blood”; the page does not make the two words one.

_own_words_why: The card's own four (Gen 9:4-6, Job 16:18) are life and bloodshed. These eight are one from each of the places the text turns on: the life in the blood, Abel's blood, the atonement, the Passover, the covenant at Sinai, the cup, Hebrews and John's letter.

_review: Reviewed 2026-10-25 by the eleven-seat panel; the fixes are in _review_2026_10_25 (two held for the editor). The builder's list of contested points, as it stood before the review: Contested points for the panel: the atonement, cleansing, justified and redeemed rows (what the blood does); 'The cup' and the covenant row (the Lord's Supper); 'The life is in the blood' (the eating of blood and Acts 15); 'In the passion' (Matt 27:25); 'The blood of Christ' and 'His blood' (the divine persons by hand); the war row's Rev 19:13. See the worker report.

rows.label: Blood that cries out: Abel's, “The earth will reveal her bloodshed”
rows.note: The blood of the murdered speaks, and the ground has received it: “The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Gen 4:10; 4:11), “O earth, do not cover my blood” (Job 16:18), “The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain” (Isa 26:21), the blood Jerusalem left on the bare rock (Ezek 24:7-8). Jesus speaks of the blood of the prophets from Abel to Zechariah (Matt 23:35; Luke 11:50-51). Heb 12:24 sets “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” beside it; what “a better word” is, readers take differently, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand (pick): Luke 11:51 and Heb 12:24 are named; Luke 11:51's clause is filed under 11:50 by the word-by-word text, so the builder cannot see the word at 11:51 and the verse is picked (read: it names the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah). Gen 4:10-11, Job 16:18 (the card's own), Isa 26:21 and Ezek 24:7-8 are the verses where the blood is the speaker or the covered thing.

rows.label: “The life is in the blood”: eating and drinking blood, and the Council's “from blood” (Acts 15)
rows.note: After the flood the first word about blood is about the life in it: “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Gen 9:4). Leviticus and Deuteronomy give the reason (“the life of the flesh is in the blood”, Lev 17:11; “the blood is the life”, Deut 12:23) and say what to do with the blood (Lev 17:13; Deut 12:16; 15:23); Saul's men eat meat with the blood and are told they are sinning (1 Sam 14:32-34); David will not drink the water brought at the risk of men's lives, and pours it out (2 Sam 23:17; 1 Chr 11:19); “Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps 50:13). In the New Testament the Council's letter lists “and from blood” among what Gentile believers should abstain from (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25). Readers part on whether that letter still binds, on whether the blood there is eaten blood or bloodshed, and on whether Gen 9:4, given before the law of Moses, binds beyond Israel; the page takes no side. Lev 17:11 is also in the atonement row. Gen 9:4-6 is one speech: its next two verses are in “Blood avenged and required” (9:5) and “Shedding blood” (9:6).
rows._why: by hand: each verse names the blood and the not eating of it, or the life that is in it. 2 Sam 23:17 and 1 Chr 11:19 are David and the water 'the blood of the men'; Ps 50:13 and Zech 9:7 are the LORD not eating blood and taking it from the mouth of the Philistines. Deut 12:24 (no blood word in the Berean's verse) fell out. Acts 15:20 reads 'and from blood' with the abstentions around it; the Berean prints 'from blood' and the page does not choose between eating and killing.

rows.label: “Flesh and blood”: a human being; and “not of blood” (John 1:13)
rows.note: The phrase for a human being: “this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood” (Matt 16:17), “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor 15:50), “our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph 6:12), “since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity” (Heb 2:14), “I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood” (Gal 1:16). John 1:13, “children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God”, does not have the phrase “flesh and blood”: it has the plural αἱμάτων, which the Berean prints “blood”, and it stands here for that word.
rows._why: by hand: the Greek has αἷμα καὶ σάρξ in Matt 16:17, 1 Cor 15:50, Gal 1:16, Eph 6:12; Heb 2:14 has the two in the other order (blood and flesh); John 1:13 has the plural αἱμάτων (the Berean prints 'not of blood') and not the phrase; it is kept in this row for the word and the label and note say so (panel, 2026-10-25).

rows.label: A flow of blood: childbirth, a woman's flow, the woman who touched His cloak
rows.note: The blood of birth and of a woman's flow, the rules for them (Lev 12; 15:19, 25; 20:18), the child “wallowing in your blood” (Ezek 16:6, 9), and the woman who “had suffered from bleeding for twelve years” (Mark 5:25-29; Luke 8:43-44). Matt 9:20 tells the same story and has no word for blood (it is the verb αἱμορροέω, named under “Other words”), so it is not in this hub's rows.
rows._why: by hand: blood as what flows from the body in birth or illness. The woman is healed in the story (Mark 5:29); the rules for her state are laws and the page says no more. Lev 15:26 (no blood word in its verse) fell out.

rows.label: Shedding blood: “by man his blood will be shed”; murder, innocent blood, hands covered with blood
rows.note: Blood as the killing of a person, in the Hebrew often the plural דָּמִים, which the Berean prints “blood” or “bloodshed”: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed” (Gen 9:6), “hands that shed innocent blood” among the things the LORD hates (Prov 6:17), “Your hands are covered with blood” (Isa 1:15), the bloody city (Ezek 22:2; Nah 3:1), “shedding the blood of the prophets” (Matt 23:30), Stephen's blood (Acts 22:20), the blood of the saints (Rev 16:6; 17:6; 18:24), Pilate's mixing of Galileans' blood with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1), and Amasa who “wallowed in his blood in the middle of the road” (2 Sam 20:12). David is told he may not build the house because “You have shed much blood and waged great wars” (1 Chr 22:8). Heb 12:4 speaks of resisting sin “to the point of shedding your blood”. In Ps 94:21 the Berean prints “condemn the innocent to death” where the Hebrew is “innocent blood”. The page lays the verses side by side and does not weigh the killing in war against the killing of a neighbor. Gen 9:4-6 is one speech: the life in the blood (9:4) is in “The life is in the blood” and the LORD's accounting (9:5) in “Blood avenged and required”. The brothers “dipped the robe in its blood”, the blood of a young goat (Gen 37:31), after their talk of Joseph's blood (37:22, 26); that verse is in “Every other use”.
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the blood is the blood of a person shed. 1 Chr 22:8 and 28:3 (David the warrior) stay, a hard verse. Luke 13:1 was in the sacrifice rows by the builder's rule (the word 'sacrifices' is there) and is held out of them: the blood is the Galileans', killed by Pilate. The guilt that follows is the next row; the LORD's avenging is the row after. A verse that says both (Deut 21:7-9, Ps 106:38) may be in two rows. Gen 9:5 ('your lifeblood is shed ... I will demand an accounting') stands in the avenged row, where it asks.

rows.label: Blood-guilt: “his blood will be on his own head”, “no bloodguilt”, “bloodshed pollutes the land”
rows.note: Blood as the guilt of a death: “his blood will be on his own head” for whoever puts himself in the way (Josh 2:19; 2 Sam 1:16; Lev 20), the owner who is free of it (Exod 22:2-3), “bloodshed pollutes the land” (Num 35:33), the city that must clear itself (Deut 21:7-9), cases of bloodshed brought to the court (Deut 17:8), David praying “Deliver me from bloodguilt” (Ps 51:14), the watchman who is held “accountable for his blood” if he does not warn (Ezek 3:18, 20; 33:4-8), Paul “innocent of the blood of all men” (Acts 20:26) and “Your blood be on your own heads!” (Acts 18:6). The same Hebrew word as the blood of the altar; the row keeps the sense apart and not the word. Pilate's “I am innocent of this man's blood” (Matt 27:24) and the council's “this man's blood” (Acts 5:28) use the same phrase and stand here; the people's answer at the trial is set only with the passion, in “In the passion”, where it has a note on how it has been read.
rows._why: by hand: the verses about the guilt and the clearing of it, not the act (the row above) nor the avenger (the row below). 2 Sam 3:29 and Num 35:26 (no blood word in their Berean verses) fell out. Matt 27:24 and Acts 5:28 carry the phrase 'this man's blood'. Matt 27:25 was here too and was taken out on the panel's word (2026-10-25: both the rabbi's seat and the young African American believer's): it stays only in the passion row, where its note stands, so a reader never meets the verse without it. Gen 42:22 'now we must account for his blood' is Reuben's, of Joseph.

rows.label: Blood avenged and required: the avenger of blood; “How long ... until You ... avenge our blood?”
rows.note: Who answers for spilled blood: the LORD says “I will demand an accounting” (Gen 9:5); “The avenger of blood is to put the murderer to death” (Num 35:19) and the cities shelter the one who killed without intent (Num 35; Deut 19; Josh 20); “the Avenger of bloodshed remembers” (Ps 9:12); the souls ask, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge those who dwell upon the earth and avenge our blood?” (Rev 6:10); and the judgment on the great prostitute: “He has avenged the blood of His servants” (Rev 19:2). Ps 72:14 says of the king that “their blood is precious in his sight”. Readers part on how these stand to one another and to the New Testament's word on vengeance; the page lays the verses side by side and takes no side. Gen 9:4-6 is one speech: the life in the blood (9:4) is in “The life is in the blood” and the shedding of blood (9:6) in “Shedding blood”.
rows._why: by hand: the avenger (גֹּאֵל) in Num 35 and Deut 19 is from the root גָּאַל, which the Old Testament also uses of the redeemer; the page does not make the two one and the row names only the avenger of blood. Ps 72:14 is also in the redeemed row; its verb is יִגְאַל (from גָּאַל 'redeem', the root of the avenger's word גֹּאֵל; corrected 2026-10-25, the earlier note said פָּדָה), and the page does not make the two words one. The panel's halves disagreed on where Ps 72:14 belongs (one asked to take it out of this row, the other out of the redeemed row), so it stays in both for the editor (see _review_2026_10_25). Joab's killing of Abner 'for the blood of Asahel' (2 Sam 3:27) is vengeance by hand and is here as the text has it.

rows.label: Blood in war and in the LORD's judgment: the slain, arrows drunk with blood, blood as high as the bridles
rows.note: “I will make My arrows drunk with blood” (Deut 32:42), “The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood” in Edom (Isa 34:6), the sword that devours “until it is quenched with their blood” (Jer 46:10), the day of the LORD pictured as a sacrifice and a feast for the birds and beasts (Isa 34:6; Jer 46:10; Ezek 39:17-19), blood on the road and on the ground where kings and the wicked fell (1 Kgs 22:35, 38; 2 Kgs 9:33), the Moabites' cry, “This is blood! The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another” (2 Kgs 3:23), “the blood that flowed from it rose as high as the bridles of the horses” (Rev 14:20), and “a robe dipped in blood” on the one whose name is The Word of God (Rev 19:13). Readers part on whose blood is on that robe (His own, the enemies', or the martyrs'), and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: blood as the outcome of war or of the LORD's judgment, in figure or in fact. Ahab's blood on the chariot and licked up by dogs (1 Kgs 22:35, 38; 21:19) is a death in battle with the word of the LORD fulfilled; Jezebel's blood on the wall (2 Kgs 9:33). Isa 63:3 (the winepress) uses another Hebrew word for the blood and is not in this hub. Isa 34:6, Jer 46:10 and Ezek 39:17, 39:19 say 'sacrifice' of the day of judgment, and are held out of the rites row for that reason. Rev 19:13: the Berean prints 'a robe dipped in blood'; the verse is hard and stays.

rows.label: Water turned to blood, the moon turned to blood: in the plagues, in the prophets, in Revelation; and water that looked like blood
rows.note: The Nile and the water of Egypt become blood (“all the water was turned to blood”, Exod 7:20; Ps 78:44; 105:29), Moses is given the sign of water that becomes blood (Exod 4:9), the water before the Moabites “looked as red as blood” (2 Kgs 3:22: an appearance, taken for blood in 3:23, which is in the war row), “the sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood” before the day of the LORD (Joel 2:31, quoted at Acts 2:20), and in Revelation “the whole moon turned blood red” (6:12), a third of the sea (8:8), the rivers and springs, “they turned to blood” (16:4), the two witnesses' power over the waters (11:6). The page connects the verses and does not read the visions. The “bridegroom of blood” of Exod 4:25-26 comes a few verses after the sign of Exod 4:9; it is in “Every other use”.
rows._why: by hand: the verses where blood is what a thing becomes or looks like (relabelled on the panel's word, 2026-10-25: 'sign' was true of Exod 4:9 and Joel, not of every verse, and 'blood in the visions' was vague; 2 Kgs 3:22 stays as an appearance). Rev 16:6 ('You have given them blood to drink') is also in the avenged row.

rows.label: The Passover: blood on the doorposts
rows.note: “The blood on the houses where you are staying will be a sign; when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exod 12:13); the blood on the sides and tops of the doorframes; and “By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood” (Heb 11:28). How the Passover and the death of Christ are related, readers take differently; the page sets the verses side by side (see sacrifice) and takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the four verses of Exod 12 that name the blood and Heb 11:28. 1 Cor 5:7 (Christ our Passover lamb) has no word for blood and is not in this hub.

rows.label: Blood in the rites of sacrifice: at the altar, sprinkled, poured out at its base

not_verses.Matt.23.35: the altar is the place where Zechariah was killed: the verse is the blood of the murdered, in 'Blood that cries out'
not_verses.Luke.11.51: the altar is the place where Zechariah was killed: the verse is the blood of the murdered, in 'Blood that cries out'
not_verses.Luke.13.1: 'sacrifices' is where the Galileans were killed by Pilate: the blood is theirs, in 'Shedding blood'
not_verses.Isa.34.6: 'a sacrifice in Bozrah' is the day of judgment pictured as a sacrifice: in 'Blood in war and in the LORD's judgment'
not_verses.Jer.46.10: 'a sacrifice in the land of the north' is the day of judgment: in 'Blood in war and in the LORD's judgment'
not_verses.Ezek.39.17: the sacrificial feast for the birds and beasts is the day of judgment: in 'Blood in war and in the LORD's judgment'
not_verses.Ezek.39.19: the sacrificial feast for the birds and beasts is the day of judgment: in 'Blood in war and in the LORD's judgment'

rows.note: The rites of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers: the priest takes the blood, “splatters it on all sides of the altar” (Lev 1:5), puts it on the horns, and pours the rest out “at the base of the altar” (Lev 4:7); the blood of the other sacrifices “must be poured out beside the altar” (Deut 12:27). The LORD says through Isaiah that He takes no pleasure in the blood of bulls, lambs and goats (Isa 1:11), and Hebrews speaks of “the blood of goats and bulls” (9:13) and of the high priest who enters “with blood that is not his own” (9:25). What the blood does in these rites is the question of the rows that follow, and the page takes no side. Ezek 44:7 is the foreigners offering “food, fat and blood” while the covenant is broken.
rows._why: by rule on the sacrifice words standing in the verse (the altar, זֶבַח, עֹלָה, שֶׁלֶם, θυσία and the rest), with the verses added by hand where the rite is in the verse and the altar or sacrifice word is in the next (Lev 4:5-6, 4:16-17: 'brings the blood into the Tent of Meeting'; Lev 6:27; 10:18; Num 19:4-5, the red heifer; 2 Chr 30:16; Ezek 44:15; Heb 9:21; Heb 10:4). חַטָּאת and אָשָׁם were first in the rule and took 'sin' as well as 'sin offering' (2 Kgs 21:16, Lam 4:13, Ezek 3:20); they are out of the rule. Seven verses held out where the altar or the sacrifice is a place or a figure.

rows.label: Blood put on or sprinkled over: the people, the ear, the thumb and the toe, the house, the tent, the scroll
rows.note: The blood is put on the person or the thing: on Aaron's right earlobe, thumb and big toe (Exod 29:20; Lev 8:23-24), on “the one to be cleansed” (Lev 14:14, 17, 25, 28), “splattered ... on the people” (Exod 24:8), on the house (Lev 14:51-52), on the tent (Heb 9:21), “the scroll and all the people” (Heb 9:19), and “sprinkling by His blood” (1 Pet 1:2).
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the blood is applied to a person or a thing and the verse says where. Lev 14:6 and 14:51-52 are the blood of the bird.

rows.label: The Day of Atonement: blood taken in before the LORD, on the mercy seat
rows.note: The blood taken inside the veil once a year: “sprinkle it with his finger on the east side of the mercy seat” (Lev 16:14), the goat's blood “behind the veil” (16:15), on the altar (16:18-19), the animals burned outside the camp (Lev 16:27; Heb 13:11). Hebrews speaks of the high priest who entered “only once a year, and never without blood” (9:7), of One who “entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood” (9:12), and of the high priest who enters “every year with blood that is not his own” (9:25). How the Day of Atonement and the death of Christ are related, readers take differently, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that name the day's rite with the blood and the Hebrews verses that speak of the same entering. Heb 9:12 says 'He'; Christ is named at 9:11.

rows.label: Blood in the worship of other gods: “libations of blood”, sons and daughters, the prophets of Baal, pig's blood
rows.note: The blood given to other gods: the prophets of Baal cutting themselves on Carmel, “until the blood gushed over them” (1 Kgs 18:28), “I will not pour out their libations of blood” (Ps 16:4), the blood of sons and daughters sacrificed to the idols of Canaan (Ps 106:38; Ezek 16:36; 23:37), and the pig's blood of Isa 66:3. That verse is a series of comparisons (“whoever presents a grain offering is like one who offers pig's blood”) said of those who “have chosen their own ways and delighted in their abominations”; it names an idol only in “blesses an idol” and does not name another god's altar. See the sacrifice page for the sons and daughters given in sacrifice.
rows._why: by hand: blood in a rite that is not the LORD's. Isa 66:3 is read as the Berean has it; the verse sets the LORD's displeasure beside offerings made by those who choose their own ways. It is a verse of comparisons and names no other god's altar; the note now says so (panel, 2026-10-25; the other option, moving it to the rites row, was not taken). 1 Kgs 18:28 is the blood of the worshipers themselves. Ps 16:4 and Isa 66:3 are the only two verses where the Hebrew names blood as the offering itself.

rows.label: Atonement and forgiveness beside blood: “it is the blood that makes atonement”, “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness”
rows.note: The text's own words: “it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul” (Lev 17:11); “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Heb 9:22); “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt 26:28); “God presented Him as an atoning sacrifice in His blood” (Rom 3:25). In Rom 3:25 the Greek word ἱλαστήριον is one readers translate “atoning sacrifice”, “propitiation”, “expiation” or “mercy seat”; it is the word for the mercy seat in Heb 9:5. Heb 10:4 is in this row for its words about taking away sins, and it denies the taking away of sins to the blood of bulls and goats: “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins”; the page takes no side on what that implies. What the blood does -- covers, pays, cleanses, turns wrath away, gives a life for a life -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. The Hebrew כִּפֶּר is a different word from the one for forgive (see forgiveness, where the two are set side by side). Atonement is also named beside the blood of the slain (Num 35:33; Deut 21:8; 32:43) and of birth (Lev 12:7). This row and the rows beside it are listed in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking.
rows._why: by rule on the atonement words in the verse (כִּפֶּר, כַּפֹּרֶת, ἱλαστήριον, ἱλασμός, ἱλάσκομαι) with the Greek by hand where the builder does not see the word: Rom 3:25 (ἱλαστήριον, the lemma the rule did not match), and the forgiveness verses (Matt 26:28, Eph 1:7, Heb 9:22: the Greek ἄφεσις; Heb 10:4: 'to take away sins'). The rule takes Num 35:33, Deut 21:8, Deut 32:43 and Lev 12:7, where atonement is named beside the blood of the slain, of the land or of birth; they are in the row because the verse names both.

rows.label: Cleansed, purified, sanctified, washed: with blood
rows.note: The altar is purified and made holy with blood (“purifying the altar”, Lev 8:15; “to cleanse it and consecrate it”, Lev 16:19; Ezek 43:20); blood is put on “the one to be cleansed” (Lev 14:14). Hebrews sets “the blood of goats and bulls” that “sanctify them so that their bodies are clean” (9:13) beside “the blood of Christ” that will “purify our consciences from works of death” (9:14); “nearly everything must be purified with blood” (9:22); “the blood of the covenant that sanctified him” (10:29), where readers part on whom “him” is and what the sanctifying was; “to sanctify the people by His own blood” (13:12); “the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7); and robes “washed ... and made ... white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14). What is cleansed -- the flesh, the conscience, the sin -- and how, readers take differently, and the page takes no side. This row and the rows beside it are listed in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking.
rows._why: by hand (pick): the verses with a word for clean, purify, sanctify or wash and the blood together. Heb 9:14's clause is filed under 9:13 by the word-by-word text, so the builder cannot see the word at 9:14 and the verse is picked (read). Lev 12:7 and 15:25, 'clean from her flow of blood', are the other sense and are in 'A flow of blood'.

rows.label: Justified, at peace, brought near, given access, overcoming: “by the blood”
rows.note: The text's own phrases: “since we have now been justified by His blood” (Rom 5:9), “making peace through the blood of His cross” (Col 1:20), “brought near through the blood of Christ” (Eph 2:13), “confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus” (Heb 10:19), “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Rev 12:11), and “an atoning sacrifice in His blood” (Rom 3:25). What the blood accomplishes in each and how the verses stand to one another, readers take differently, and the page takes no side. This row and the rows beside it are listed in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking.
rows._why: by hand: what the verse says the blood brings about, other than forgiveness, cleansing or redemption (the rows beside it). Rom 3:25 is also in the atonement row.

rows.label: Redeemed, purchased, released: “by Your blood You purchased for God”
rows.note: Ps 72:14, the king “will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight”; the blood there is the poor's own, precious to the king, and the verse does not name blood as a price paid (its Hebrew verb is יִגְאַל, from גָּאַל “redeem”, the root of the avenger's word in Num 35; the page does not make the two words one). And in the New Testament, “redemption through His blood” (Eph 1:7), “securing eternal redemption” (Heb 9:12), “the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Pet 1:19), “has released us from our sins by His blood” (Rev 1:5), “by Your blood You purchased for God” (Rev 5:9), “which He purchased with His own blood” (Acts 20:28). In Acts 20:28 the Greek reads “through the blood the own” and can be taken as “His own blood” or “the blood of His Own”; readers part on it, and on whom the verse means by God, and the page does not choose. Who is paid, from what, and what the price is, readers take differently, and the page takes no side. This row and the rows beside it are listed in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking.
rows._why: by hand: the verses with a word for redeem, purchase or release and the blood together. The Hebrew גָּאַל 'redeem' (Lev 25) has no verse with דָּם except Ps 72:14, whose verb is יִגְאַל (from גָּאַל; the earlier note here said it had none, and the panel found the error, 2026-10-25); Ps 72:14 is here and in the avenged row, and its placement is for the editor (halves of the panel asked opposite removals). Deut 21:8 ('Your people ... whom You redeemed') says redeemed of Egypt and blood of the innocent: it is in the atonement and guilt rows.

rows.label: The blood of the covenant

not_verses.Ezek.44.7: foreigners offering 'food, fat and blood' while breaking the covenant: the blood is the offering, not the covenant's; it is in 'Blood in the rites of sacrifice'

rows.note: “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exod 24:8), “because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit” (Zech 9:11), “This is My blood of the covenant” (Matt 26:28; Mark 14:24), “the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20; 1 Cor 11:25), “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep” (Heb 9:20), “the first covenant was not put into effect without blood” (Heb 9:18), “the blood of the covenant that sanctified him” (Heb 10:29) and “the blood of the eternal covenant” (13:20). Exod 24:6 puts half of the blood in bowls and half on the altar, before the covenant is named. How the covenants relate (one in many forms, or several; the old and the new) and how the cup stands to them, readers take differently, and the page takes no side (see covenant).
rows._why: by rule on בְּרִית and διαθήκη in the verse, with Exod 24:6 and Heb 9:18 by hand (Heb 9:18's Berean 'first covenant' has no noun in the Greek: 'the first' only, as the covenant hub says). The rule also took Ezek 44:7; held out.

rows.label: The cup: “This is My blood”, “the cup of blessing”, “a participation in the blood of Christ”
rows.note: The words of the Last Supper (Matt 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20) and of Paul on the cup (“This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me”, 1 Cor 11:25; “guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord”, 11:27; “Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ?”, 10:16). Where Christian traditions part on what the cup is -- the blood of Christ really present, a memorial, a participation in Christ, or something more -- and on how the cup stands to sacrifice (see sacrifice), the page takes no side. The saying at Capernaum (John 6:53-56), which readers part on whether it speaks of the Supper, is in the row after this one. The Berean notes that some manuscripts do not include Luke 22:20; the page takes no side on that either.
rows._why: by hand, the verses that speak of the cup and the blood together: the owner's contested list names 'the Lord's Supper ('this is my blood': what is called real presence, the memorial reading and others)'. 1 Cor 11:27 is 'guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord'; 1 Cor 11:25 has 'do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me' in the same verse as the blood, and the page does not read it. Mark 14:24 'This is My blood of the covenant'. John 6:53-56 were in this row (label 'drink My blood') and were moved to their own row on the panel's word (2026-10-25, both halves: placing the saying under the cup settled by row order what the note said readers part on).

rows.label: Eating the flesh and drinking the blood: the saying at Capernaum (John 6)
rows.note: Jesus at Capernaum: “unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you” (John 6:53), “Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life” (6:54), “My blood is real drink” (6:55), and 6:56. These verses name no cup and no Supper; they stand here for the words “drink the blood”. Readers part on whether the saying speaks of the Lord's Supper or of something else, and the page takes no side. The cup of the Supper (Matt 26:28; 1 Cor 10:16; 11:25) is in the row before this one.
rows._why: by hand: John 6:53-56, the saying at Capernaum whose Greek is 'drink the blood'. Moved out of 'The cup' (panel, both halves, 2026-10-25) so that no row order settles whether John 6 speaks of the Supper. No door to the Last Supper, for the same reason.

rows.label: The blood of Christ, of Jesus, of the Son, of the Lamb
rows.note: Each verse names him: “the blood of Christ” (1 Cor 10:16; Eph 2:13; Heb 9:14; 1 Pet 1:19), “the blood of Jesus” (Heb 10:19), “the Son of God ... the blood of the covenant” (Heb 10:29), “Jesus ... His own blood” (Heb 13:12), “the blood of the eternal covenant” of “our Lord Jesus” (13:20), “sprinkling by His blood” for “Jesus Christ” (1 Pet 1:2), “the blood of Jesus His Son” (1 John 1:7), “Jesus Christ ... by water and blood” (1 John 5:6), “Jesus Christ ... by His blood” (Rev 1:5), “the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14; 12:11). Five verses say only “His blood”, “His own blood” or “Your blood”; each is shown here with the verse beside it that answers the pronoun: Rom 3:25, “God presented Him as an atoning sacrifice in His blood”, after Rom 3:24, “the redemption that is in Christ Jesus”; Rom 5:9, “justified by His blood”, after Rom 5:8, “Christ died for us”; Eph 1:7, “redemption through His blood”, after Eph 1:6, “in the Beloved One”; Heb 9:12, “His own blood”, after Heb 9:11, “Christ came as high priest”; Rev 5:9, “by Your blood You purchased for God”, after Rev 5:8, “fell down before the Lamb”. Every verse in this row names him, or the verse beside it does. Col 1:20 and Acts 20:28 are in the next row. The cup of the Supper (“My blood”) is in the cup row.
rows._why: by hand (divine persons by hand): every verse names Christ, Jesus, the Son or the Lamb in the verse itself, or has the verse beside it that does. 'The Lamb' is the text's own title in Revelation and the page does not add a name. Heb 9:14 is picked because the builder cannot see the word there (its clause is filed under 9:13). Rom 3:25, 5:9, Eph 1:7, Heb 9:12 and Rev 5:9 were in the pronoun row (the rulings sheet, 2026-10-25, merged them in part): each is picked here with the neighbouring verse read in the Berean that answers the pronoun (Rom 3:24 'Christ Jesus', Rom 5:8 'Christ', Eph 1:6 'the Beloved One', Heb 9:11 'Christ', Rev 5:8 'the Lamb'); those five neighbouring verses hold no word for blood and are shown for the name. Col 1:19, beside Col 1:20, says only 'Him' again, and Acts 20:28 names God, so those two stay in the pronoun row.

rows.label: “The blood of His cross”, “His own blood”: the verse beside Col 1:20 does not name him; Acts 20:28 names God
rows.note: Two verses. Col 1:20 says “by making peace through the blood of His cross”; the verse beside it, Col 1:19, “For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him”, says only “Him” and does not name the one whose cross it is. Acts 20:28 reads “Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood”: it names God. In the Greek it is “through the blood the own”, and it can be taken as “His own blood” or “the blood of His Own”; readers part on it, and on whom the verse means by God, and the page does not choose. The other verses that say “His blood”, “His own blood” or “Your blood” are in the row about the blood of Christ, each with the verse beside it that names him.
rows._why: by hand (divine persons by hand): the pronoun without a name. Rom 3:25, 5:9, Eph 1:7, Heb 9:12 and Rev 5:9 moved to the Christ row on the rulings sheet (Doug, 2026-10-25, as recommended), each with the verse beside it that answers the pronoun. Col 1:19 (read in the Berean) says only 'Him' again and does not name him; Acts 20:28 names God and is read two ways. Both verses stay in their other rows too (Col 1:20 in 'Justified, at peace, brought near'; Acts 20:28 in 'Redeemed, purchased, released'). The next-door verses are given in the note, not placed in the row.

rows.label: In the passion: Gethsemane, innocent blood, “blood money”, the Field of Blood, “His blood be on us”, blood and water
rows.note: Judas, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt 27:4), the chief priests who say it is “blood money” (27:6) and buy the field called the Field of Blood (27:8; Acts 1:19), Pilate who washes his hands, “I am innocent of this man's blood” (27:24), the people's answer, “His blood be on us and on our children!” (27:25), the council's charge that “you ... are determined to make us responsible for this man's blood” (Acts 5:28), “His sweat became like drops of blood” (Luke 22:44, which some manuscripts do not include), the spear and “blood and water” (John 19:34), and “the One who came by water and blood” (1 John 5:6, 8). Matt 27:25 has been read against the Jewish people; readers part sharply on what the verse says of anyone beyond those who spoke it, and the page sets it in the text's own words with Pilate's and says no more. What the water and the blood mean in John 19:34 and 1 John 5:6, readers also take differently.
rows._why: by hand: the verses of the passion and its aftermath where the blood is Jesus' own death or its price. Matt 27:25 is the hard verse, kept, with the note a rabbi's seat and a young African American believer's would want (it has a history of being turned on a people); it was also in the blood-guilt row, as the same idiom, and was taken out of it on the panel's word (2026-10-25), so it stands only here. Luke 22:44 was in 'Every other use' (the Berean notes 'Some manuscripts do not include verses 43 and 44').

rows.label: Every other use
rows.note: Among them, Joseph's robe, where they “dipped the robe in its blood” (Gen 37:31), Zipporah's “bridegroom of blood” (Exod 4:25-26), “his robes in the blood of grapes” (Gen 49:11), the bird whose “young ones feast on blood” (Job 39:30), “What gain is there in my bloodshed, in my descent to the Pit?” (Ps 30:9), and “the twisting of the nose draws blood” (Prov 30:33). Three verses where the Berean's English has no “blood”: Deut 32:14 (“the juice of the finest grapes”; the Hebrew is “blood of the grape”), Lev 19:16 (“endanger the life of your neighbor”; the Hebrew says “the blood of your neighbor”) and Ezek 19:10, where the Berean reads “vineyard” and notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read “in your bloodline”.
rows._why: the catch-all: what no other row takes. Found in the 16-verse check: Deut 32:14, Lev 19:16 and Ezek 19:10 have the Hebrew word and not the English one, and say so here; Ps 94:21 ('condemn the innocent to death', Hebrew 'innocent blood') is in the shedding row for the same reason, and its note says so.
